entry: Science and art of growing ornamental plants, flowers, fruits, vegetables and other economically valuable crops or trees on a controlled scale. Horticulture is distinct from conventional extensive farming and row-crop [[Agronomy|agronomy]] through its emphasis on landscaping, plant propagation, floriculture and crops grown in greenhouses or other controlled environments. Its divisions include propagation, arboriculture, landscaping, floriculture and turf maintenance, and its practitioners range from growers and farmers to landscape architects and botanical garden curators. Horticulture differs from [[Gardening|gardening]] in its emphasis on scientific methods, plant breeding and technical cultivation practices. It began with the [[Domestication|domestication]] of plants c. 10,000–20,000 years ago, and it emerged as a field distinct from agriculture when humans grew plants for pleasure on a smaller scale. Modifying technologies such as [[CRISPR]] are improving the nutrition, taste and yield of crops, while emerging technologies make plants more resistant to parasites, disease and drought.

Ancient Egyptian god of kingship, healing, protection, the sun and the sky. Worshipped from at least the late prehistoric period until the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]] and Roman Egypt, Horus was most often depicted as a [[Falcon|falcon]] or as a man with a falcon head. The earliest recorded form was the tutelary deity of Nekhen in Upper Egypt, regarded as the first known national god. The pharaoh was identified with Horus in life and with [[Osiris]] in death, and was also seen as the son of [[Ra]]. In the most common account, Horus is the son of [[Isis]] and Osiris, and he avenges his father against [[Set (deity)|Set]], the murderer and brother of Osiris. Other traditions make [[Hathor]] his mother and sometimes his wife. The Roman writer Claudius Aelianus reported that Egyptians called [[Apollo]] "Horus" in their own language.

Lighter-than-air [[Aircraft|aircraft]] consisting of a bag, or envelope, of heated air with a gondola or wicker basket suspended beneath it. The heated air inside the envelope is less dense than the colder air outside, which makes the envelope [[Buoyancy|buoyant]]. The gondola carries passengers and a source of heat, usually an open flame fueled by liquid [[Propane]]. Modern sport envelopes are generally made of [[Nylon]] fabric. Balloons that are not propelled drift with the wind; those that can be propelled are called thermal airships. The hot air balloon is the first successful human-carrying flight technology. Its precursor, the sky lantern, was used for military signaling by [[Zhuge Liang]] of the Shu Han kingdom during the [[Three Kingdoms]] era (220–280 CE). The first untethered manned flight was made in [[Paris]] on November 21, 1783, by Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent d'Arlandes, in a balloon built by the [[Montgolfier brothers]].

Grilled, steamed or boiled [[Sausage|sausage]] served in the slit of a partially sliced bun. The sausage used is a wiener or frankfurter, types that were culturally imported from [[Germany]] and became popular in the [[United States]]. It became a working-class street food sold at stands and carts. Common condiments include [[Mustard (condiment)|mustard]], [[Ketchup|ketchup]], relish and cheese sauce. The hot dog is closely associated with [[Baseball|baseball]] and [[New York City]], and during the 20th century it became ubiquitous throughout the U.S. It is not definitively known who first served the sausage in a bun.

Spring produced by the emergence of geothermally heated [[Groundwater|groundwater]] onto the surface of the Earth. The water is heated either by shallow bodies of [[Magma|magma]] or by circulation along faults to hot rock deep in the Earth's crust. A spring that periodically jets water and steam is called a [[Geyser|geyser]]. Hot spring water often contains large amounts of dissolved [[Mineral|minerals]], and its chemistry ranges from acid sulfate springs with a pH as low as 0.8 to alkaline chloride springs saturated with silica. These minerals often feed communities of [[Extremophile|extremophiles]], and it is possible that life on Earth had its origin in hot springs. People have used them for bathing, relaxation and medical therapy for thousands of years, though some are hot enough that immersion can cause scalding and death.

Establishment providing paid lodging on a short-term basis. Rooms may range from a modest mattress in a small room to large suites with a dresser, a [[Refrigerator|refrigerator]], [[Chair|upholstered chairs]], a television and en-suite bathrooms. Larger hotels may add a [[Swimming pool|swimming pool]], a business center, conference facilities, childcare, [[Restaurant|restaurants]] and a day spa. The precursor of the modern hotel was the inn of medieval Europe, and coaching inns served coach travelers for about 200 years from the mid-17th century. One of the first hotels in the modern sense opened in Exeter in 1768. Hotels proliferated throughout [[Western Europe]] and [[North America]] in the early 19th century, and luxury hotels spread in the later 19th century, particularly in the [[United States]]. Classifications range from economy hotels offering basic accommodation to upscale full-service hotels with a concierge and room service.

Rock song by the American band [[Eagles (band)|Eagles]]. Written by Don Felder, Glenn Frey and Don Henley, it was the second single from the 1976 album *Hotel California*, released on February 22, 1977. Henley sings lead, and the song ends with a long [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]] solo by Felder and Joe Walsh. It reached number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and won the Grammy Award for Record of the Year in 1978. The band described it as their "interpretation of the high life in [[Los Angeles]]", and its lyrics have prompted many interpretations.

Volcanic locale in [[Geology|geology]], fed by underlying [[Earth's mantle|mantle]] that is anomalously hot compared with the surrounding mantle. Hotspots are independent of tectonic plate boundaries, so as plates move over them they may create a chain of [[Volcano|volcanoes]], as in the [[Hawaiian Islands]]. Two [[Hypothesis|hypotheses]] explain their origin. One holds that mantle plumes rise as thermal diapirs from the core–mantle boundary; the other holds that the crust above is unusually weak or thin, so that melt rises passively from shallow depths. Estimates of plume-fed hotspots range from about 20 to several thousand, with most geologists considering a few dozen to exist. Most hotspot volcanoes are [[Basalt|basaltic]] and so less explosive than subduction-zone volcanoes, although under continents the Yellowstone Caldera was formed by some of the most powerful volcanic explosions in geologic history.

Type of hunting dog used to track or chase prey. Hounds are a diverse group, all bred specifically for hunting, and they have either a powerful sense of smell, great speed, or both. Sighthounds, also called gazehounds, follow prey mainly by speed and keep it in sight. They are fast and were used to catch game such as [[Fox|fox]], [[Hare|hare]], [[Deer|deer]] and [[Elk|elk]], and they include the [[Greyhound]]. Scenthounds track prey, or missing people, by scent; they have endurance but are not fast runners, and they include the [[Bloodhound]] and [[Beagle]]. Some breeds follow prey by both sight and scent and are difficult to classify. Hounds are contrasted with [[Gun dog|gun dogs]], which identify prey or recover shot quarry.

Unit of time equal to 60 minutes, defined as exactly 3,600 seconds. Historically reckoned as 1⁄24 of a day, the hour was first established in the ancient Near East as a variable measure of 1⁄12 of the night or daytime, which varied by season and [[Latitude|latitude]]. Egyptians and Greeks divided the day into 12 seasonal hours. By the [[Hellenistic period]] the night was also divided into 12 hours, and the day and night were probably first divided into 24 hours by [[Hipparchus]] of Nicaea. Equal hours were later taken as 1⁄24 of the mean solar day, and the unit was eventually defined in terms of the atomic or physical [[Second|second]]. Decimal time was briefly tried during the [[French Revolution]], but the 24-hour system persists. The English word derives from Anglo-Norman *houre*, first attested in the 13th century, and is distantly cognate with [[Year|year]].

American medical drama television series (2004–2012). Created by David Shore for [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]], it aired for eight seasons from November 16, 2004, to May 21, 2012. [[Hugh Laurie]] plays Dr. Gregory House, an unconventional and misanthropic medical genius who leads a diagnostic team at the fictional Princeton–Plainsboro Teaching Hospital in New Jersey. The series was among the top 10 in the United States from its second through fourth seasons and won five Primetime Emmy Awards, two Golden Globe Awards and a Peabody Award. Fox announced in February 2012 that the eighth season would be its last.

Residential building, ranging from a rudimentary hut to a complex structure of wood, masonry or concrete. Houses are outfitted with plumbing, electrical, and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems, and have doors or locks to protect their occupants from trespassers. Most conventional modern houses in Western cultures contain one or more [[Bedroom|bedrooms]] and [[Bathroom|bathrooms]], a [[Kitchen|kitchen]] or cooking area, and a living room. The social unit that lives in a house is a [[Household|household]], most commonly a family. Larger townhouses or row houses may contain numerous dwellings in one structure. A house may be accompanied by outbuildings such as a [[Garage (residential)|garage]] or shed, and by a backyard or front yard. The English word derives from Old English *hus*, meaning dwelling, shelter, home, house.

Small [[Mammal|mammal]] (*Mus musculus*) of the [[Rodent|rodent]] family [[Muridae]]. Although a wild animal, it has benefited greatly from association with human habitation, to the point that truly wild populations are much less common than those near human activity. It has a pointed snout, large rounded ears and a long, almost hairless tail, and its adult body length is 7.5–10 cm. It has been domesticated as the pet or fancy mouse and as the laboratory mouse, one of the most important [[Model organism|model organisms]] in biology and medicine. The complete mouse reference genome was sequenced in 2002.

Cadet branch of the [[Capetian dynasty]], the royal house of France. Bourbon kings first ruled France and Navarre in the 16th century, beginning with [[Henry IV of France|Henry IV]] in 1589. A Spanish branch, descended from [[Philip V of Spain]], succeeded the childless [[Charles II of Spain]] in 1700 and has reigned in Spain for 1700–1808, 1813–1868, 1875–1931 and since 1975. The senior French line was overthrown in 1792 during the [[French Revolution]], restored in 1815 after the fall of the [[First French Empire]], and overthrown again in the [[July Revolution]] of 1830. Spain and Luxembourg have monarchs from the House of Bourbon.

sort_key: house of cards american tv series
entry: American political thriller television series (2013–2018). Created by Beau Willimon for [[Netflix]], it is based on the 1989 novel by Michael Dobbs. [[Kevin Spacey]] plays Frank Underwood, a Democrat from South Carolina who is passed over for Secretary of State and schemes for power with his wife, Claire, played by Robin Wright. Set in [[Washington, D.C.]], the series received 33 Primetime Emmy Award nominations and won Golden Globes for Wright and Spacey. In 2017, after allegations of sexual misconduct against Spacey, which he has denied, Netflix ended its relationship with him. The sixth and final season was released in 2018 without him.

headword: House of Commons of the United Kingdom
sort_key: house of commons of the united kingdom
entry: Lower house of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]]. Its 650 members of Parliament (MPs) are elected by first-past-the-post voting to represent constituencies. The Commons meets in the [[Palace of Westminster]] in London. It began to evolve in the 13th and 14th centuries, became the House of Commons of Great Britain in 1707 after the union with Scotland, and in 1922 became the House of Commons of the United Kingdom. Although the House does not formally elect the prime minister, the prime minister must keep its support, and the Commons may remove a government by passing a motion of no confidence.

Dynasty, also known as the House of Austria, that ruled vast realms in Europe and the Americas. The name derives from Habsburg Castle, a fortress built in the 1020s in present-day Switzerland. In 1273 Rudolph, a descendant of the fortress's builder, was elected King of the Romans. After defeating Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278, he moved the family's power base to [[Vienna]], where the dynasty ruled until 1918. The Habsburgs occupied the throne of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] until their male line ended in 1740, and their Habsburg-Lorraine descendants held it until the empire's dissolution in 1806. After the abdication of Emperor Charles V in 1556, the family split into Spanish and German-Austrian branches that often intermarried. The Spanish line ended in 1700 with the childless death of Charles II, amid the dynasty's [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]].

Upper house of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]], which meets in the [[Palace of Westminster]] in London. Most of its members are appointed for life as peers, and up to 26 archbishops and bishops of the [[Church of England]] sit as Lords Spiritual. Hereditary peers, once the majority, were limited to 92 from 1999 and abolished altogether in 2026. The Lords can delay bills for up to one year but, except in limited circumstances, cannot prevent them from becoming law. It is the only upper house of any bicameral parliament in the world that is larger than its lower house.

Italian banking family and political dynasty in [[Florence]]. The family came from the Mugello region of [[Tuscany]] and initially drew its wealth from the wool trade. The Medici Bank, created in 1397, was Europe's largest in the 15th century and helped the family gain political power in Florence, though the Medici officially remained citizens rather than monarchs until the 16th century. In 1532 the family acquired the hereditary title Duke of Florence, and in 1569 the duchy became the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, which the Medici ruled until 1737. The family produced four [[Pope|popes]] and two queens of [[France]]. It patronized [[Donatello]], [[Michelangelo]] and [[Leonardo da Vinci]], and financed the construction of [[Florence Cathedral]].

Angevin royal dynasty that ruled England from 1154 to 1485. The family originated in the French county of Anjou, and its first three kings also ruled extensive territories in France, including [[Normandy]]. The Plantagenets were often forced to compromise, as in [[Magna Carta]], which constrained royal power in return for financial and military support. By the end of the reign of [[Edward III]] (r. 1327–1377), the dynasty had adopted [[Middle English]] as the language of governance. In the 15th century the Plantagenets lost the [[Hundred Years' War]] and fell into conflict between the cadet branches of Lancaster and York, which fought the [[Wars of the Roses]]. The dynasty ended at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, when Richard III died and Henry VII, who married Elizabeth of York, founded the Tudor dynasty. Every monarch of England and of the [[United Kingdom]] since Henry VII descends from the Plantagenets.

Imperial dynasty of Russia, 1613–1917. The family rose to prominence when Anastasia Romanovna married [[Ivan the Terrible]]. The Zemsky Sobor elected Michael Romanov as tsar on February 21, 1613, after the Time of Troubles, establishing the Romanovs as Russia's second reigning dynasty. Michael's grandson, [[Peter the Great]], proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. The direct male line ended when Elizabeth died childless in 1762; later monarchs claimed the throne through the Holstein-Gottorp branch, though the Romanov name remained in official use. [[Nicholas II]] abdicated in March 1917 during the February Revolution, ending 304 years of Romanov rule. In 1918 the Bolsheviks executed him and his family at [[Yekaterinburg]], and 47 survivors of the house's 65 members went into exile abroad.

Ruling royal family of [[Saudi Arabia]], descended from Muhammad bin Saud and his brothers. The king is an [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarch]]. Of an estimated 15,000 members, about 2,000 hold most of the power, influence and wealth, and some estimates put the family's net worth at $1.4 trillion, including the market capitalization of [[Saudi Aramco]]. The current state, dating from 1902, evolved into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932 under [[Ibn Saud]]. Succession passed by agnatic seniority until 2006, when a royal decree provided for kings to be elected by a committee of princes. In 2017 [[Mohammed bin Salman]] became crown prince.

English royal house of Welsh origin, ruling 1485–1603. Henry VII took the throne by conquest at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, then married Elizabeth of York, ending the [[Wars of the Roses]]. The dynasty succeeded the [[House of Plantagenet]] and produced five monarchs, including [[Henry VIII]], whose reign began the English Reformation. [[Elizabeth I]] was the longest-serving Tudor monarch, reigning 44 years, and her rule consolidated the [[Church of England]]. When Elizabeth died childless in 1603, the Scottish [[James VI and I]] succeeded her.

Abbasid-era public library and intellectual center in [[Baghdad]], also called the Grand Library of Baghdad. It began as a library for the collections of Caliph [[Harun al-Rashid]] (r. 786–809), and under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) it became a public academy and library. Translators there rendered Greek, Syriac, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, including texts by [[Aristotle]], [[Plato]], [[Galen]], [[Hippocrates]] and [[Euclid]], as part of the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. The house was destroyed in 1258 during the Mongol siege of Baghdad. Some historians argue that its image as a university with specialized departments was constructed by 19th- and early 20th-century Orientalist scholars through translation errors and retrospective projection.

Small [[Bird|bird]] of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world. Typically 16 cm (6.3 in) long with a mass of 24–39.5 g, it is native to most of Europe, the Mediterranean Basin and a large part of Asia. Introductions have carried it to parts of Australasia, Africa and the Americas, making it the most widely distributed wild bird. Males have brighter black, white and brown markings, while females and young birds are pale brown and gray. The house sparrow is strongly associated with human habitation, feeding on seeds, grains and [[Weed|weeds]] as well as [[Insect|insects]] and their larvae. It has often been kept as a pet and is extensively persecuted as an agricultural pest, usually unsuccessfully. It is one of 28 [[Species|species]] in the genus *Passer*, and the IUCN lists it as least concern.
